extracted.intended_audience: teachers, educators, students of education, and those studying logic or the scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for instructing and practicing systematic thinking (induction and deduction), including how to form, test, and teach hypotheses and how to structure observation, experiment, and reasoning. Emphasis is educational application and methods for regulating thought processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concluding step: experimental corroboration (verification)
rubrics_metrics.description: The concluding and conclusive step is some kind of experimental corroboration, or verification, of the conjectural idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasoning shows that if the idea is adopted certain consequences follow; observation or deliberate experiment must then test whether the conditions and characteristic traits predicted by the hypothesis are present. If experimental results agree with the theoretically deduced results, and if only the tested conditions would yield such results, the confirmation is strong enough to induce acceptance—at least until contrary facts indicate revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation at the termini of thinking
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation exists at the beginning and again at the end of the process: at the beginning to determine the nature of the difficulty; at the end to test the value of a hypothetically entertained conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Between these observations lie inference (suggestion of an explanation) and reasoning (development of implications). Reasoning requires experimental observation to confirm it, while experiment is most fruitful when guided by ideas developed by reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trained mind judges extent of each step
rubrics_metrics.description: The disciplined, or logically trained, mind is able to judge how far each of the steps (observation, forming ideas, reasoning, experimental testing) needs to be carried in any particular situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No fixed rules apply; each case must be handled according to its importance and context. Too much or too little effort is illogical. A trained mind senses problems, chooses appropriate methods of attack, and profits from past mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double movement of reflection: induction and deduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Reflection involves a double movement: (1) from partial, confused data to a suggested comprehensive meaning (induction), and (2) back from the suggested whole to particular facts (deduction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A complete act of thought requires both movements interacting fruitfully: induction for discovery of a binding principle; deduction for testing and developing that principle into particulars. The movement may be casual or cautious; disciplined thought insists on stating connecting links (universals) and tracing reasoning steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction as discovery; deduction as testing/elaboration
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction (inductive discovery) moves from particulars to a connected view (universal). Deduction (deductive proof) begins with the universal and works back to particulars to test and develop the idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Induction suggests and frames hypotheses as working hypotheses; deduction elaborates their bearings and predicts consequences which must be confirmed by observation or experiment. Valid discovery arises when the two are conducted in the light of one another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance of the inductive movement is indirect
rubrics_metrics.description: Control of the formation of suggestion is necessarily indirect and imperfect—suggestions originate from past experience, temperament, training, and chance circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indirect control is possible by cultivating patience, suspended judgment, and a liking for inquiry, and by revising and analyzing the facts out of which suggestions spring. Methods include carefully inventorying facts, enlarging the scope of data, and rendering details more minute so that different suggestions may be induced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific induction: regulating observation and data-collection
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific induction consists of all processes by which observing and amassing of data are regulated to facilitate the formation of explanatory conceptions and theories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifically, selective determination in induction involves: (1) elimination by analysis of what is likely to be misleading and irrelevant; (2) emphasis of the important by collection and comparison of cases; and (3) deliberate construction of data by experimental variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elimination of irrelevant meanings (guard against premature interpretation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The observer should discriminate between observed facts and judgments based upon them, eliminating those inferences with greatest liability to error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This involves checking habitual readings of situations, being on guard against errors from interests, preconceptions, and excitement, and using instruments and permanent records (thermometers, photographs, kymographs, etc.) to give objective data that different persons can verify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collection of instances: multiply cases and emphasize contrast
rubrics_metrics.description: Another method of control is the multiplication of cases—collecting and comparing multiple instances to secure a sound induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparison without contrast is insufficient: unlikeness among cases is as important as likeness. Select extreme or varied cases so differences highlight significant factors. The object of many cases is to help select the evidential features for inference in a single case. Methods of agreement (comparison) and difference (contrast) must accompany each other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of exceptions and contrary cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Anomalies, exceptions, and contrary instances are crucial; scientists design techniques to detect, record, and remember contrasting cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively hunt for contrary instances; record exceptions (Darwin's practice) because opposing cases often reveal flaws in favored generalizations and are easily overlooked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental variation: deliberate construction of crucial cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimentation is the construction, by regular steps taken on a plan, of a typical, crucial case formed to shed light on the difficulty at hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiment overcomes defects due to rarity, subtlety/minuteness, and rigid fixity of ordinary facts. By varying conditions one can reveal phenomena otherwise obscure and produce cases of the 'right kind' for sound inference; much of inductive method reduces to experimental variation when feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance of the deductive movement: systematized knowledge and elaboration
rubrics_metrics.description: Deduction requires possession of a body of general principles that can be applied to examine or construct particular cases and to elaborate inchoate ideas into fuller meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematic allied ideas, definitions, general formulae, and classifications allow substitutions and graded steps so that deductions can trace remote consequences. Deduction indicates what features are significant, locates and defines the nature of a problem, and suggests further observations to test the idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final control of deduction: experimental observation
rubrics_metrics.description: The ultimate test of deduction lies in experimental observation: elaboration by reasoning must be followed by observation or experiment to settle validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even rich and plausible deductive developments are incomplete without observed facts that agree in detail and without exception with the deduced results. Thinking must both begin and end in concrete observation to be complete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educational bearings: avoid isolating facts or isolated deduction; require active elaboration by students
rubrics_metrics.description: Educational practice should not treat induction as mere amassing of facts nor treat deduction as complete in itself; students should be trained to form and then elaborate suggestions into reasoned conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid: (i) immersing pupils in disconnected details without relating them to larger situations; (ii) accepting students' guesses without requiring them to develop the idea; (iii) beginning instruction solely with definitions and general principles (isolating deduction). Instead, have learners be responsible for elaborating their own suggestions, follow up reasoning, and see how particulars are bound together, so that learning is more than a 'scrap-bag' of facts.
